In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Guatemalan and Peruvian Truth Commissions, in their respective final reports, have not been able to fully recognize the victims of the conflict, in the sense that the latter have been denied the status of victims, and have been excluded from the categories of victims, as well as from the categories of perpetrators, in the final reports.

the Guatemalan and the Peruvian truth commissions have failed in their attempt to provide the victims of state violence with a space for the recognition of their rights and the acknowledgement of their suffering.

the two Truth Commissions in Guatemala and Peru, as well as the academic debates that preceded their work, reveal the complex relation between indianity and politics, a relation that has deep historical roots.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the testimonial policy of the Guatemalan Truth Commission (CEH) and the Peruvian Truth and Reconciliation Commission (CVR) was based on a racialized and gendered interpretation of the conflict that affected indigenous populations in both countries.
we are interested in understanding how the Guatemalan Truth Commission and the Peruvian Truth Commission (1990s) have been dealing with the indigenous peoples' testimonies.
we are concerned with the politics of testimony and recognition in the truth commissions of Guatemala and Peru.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the testimonies and the narratives produced in both truth commissions were not only a means of establishing a record of the past, but also a means to produce a new political subjectivity.

the politics of testimony and recognition in the Guatemalan and Peruvian Truth Commissions, as they are reflected in the final reports of both Commissions, is deeply influenced by the narratives of the indigenous people that are used to understand the violence in both countries.

the testimonial practices in the Guatemalan and Peruvian Commissions of the Truth are not only about the production of knowledge about violence, but are also about the construction of a political space of citizenship in which the victims and the perpetrators of violence are given the chance to participate
